title: Base-b Divisibility Rules
description: Generalizes divisibility rules to arbitrary bases: for b ≥ 3, (b-1) | n iff (b-1) | digit_sum_b(n). Covers hexadecimal (mod 15), octal (mod 7), factor tests, and cross-base divisibility. All 15 theorems fully verified.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules are among the oldest techniques in arithmetic, with the rule for 9 (casting out nines) described by al-Khwarizmi in the 9th century and widely used in medieval European arithmetic for error checking. The underlying principle — that $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ makes digit sums preserve residues — was understood implicitly long before modular arithmetic was formalized by Gauss in *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801). This formalization generalizes the base-10 rule to arbitrary bases, revealing the universal structure: for any base $b \ge 3$, the digit sum test works modulo $b-1$ and all its divisors. The hex (base 16) case is practically important in computing, where divisibility by 15, 5, or 3 can be checked via hex digit sums. The cross-base theorem — that the same divisibility test works in any base where $d | (b-1)$ — unifies all these rules into a single principle.
overview.problemStatement:
**Base-b Divisibility Rules:**

For b ≥ 3 and n ∈ ℕ:
$$n \equiv \sum_i d_i \pmod{b-1}$$
where $d_i$ are the base-b digits of n.

More generally, for any d ≥ 2 dividing (b-1):
$$d \mid n \iff d \mid \sum_i d_i$$
overview.proofStrategy: The key observation is b ≡ 1 (mod b-1), proved by Euclidean division: b = (b-1)·1 + 1. Then b^k ≡ 1^k = 1 (mod b-1), so n = Σ dᵢ·b^i ≡ Σ dᵢ (mod b-1). For factors d of (b-1), the same logic applies since b ≡ 1 (mod d).
keyInsights: The single identity $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ is the universal engine: since $b^k \equiv 1^k = 1$, the positional value of each digit is erased mod $(b-1)$, collapsing $n = \sum d_i b^i$ to $n \equiv \sum d_i$

Factor divisibility follows automatically: if $d | (b-1)$ then $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, so the digit sum test works for $d$ too. This explains why 3 divides $n$ iff 3 divides the digit sum in base 10 (since $3 | 9$), base 16 (since $3 | 15$), or base 7 (since $3 | 6$)

The cross-base theorem is remarkably elegant: if $d | (b_1 - 1)$ and $d | (b_2 - 1)$, then $d | \text{digitsum}_{b_1}(n) \iff d | \text{digitsum}_{b_2}(n)$ — the divisibility test is base-independent, depending only on the relationship between $d$ and the base

The proof is extremely concise because it delegates to Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` and `Nat.dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum`, which handle the digit decomposition; the contribution is the modular arithmetic setup ($b \% (b-1) = 1$) and the systematic specialization to practical bases
Numerical examples use `native_decide` for efficient verification: e.g., $255 = \text{0xFF}$ has hex digit sum $15 + 15 = 30$, and $15 | 30$ confirms $15 | 255$

sections.title: Documentation and Imports
sections.summary: Detailed header documenting the generalization approach, status checklist, and Mathlib dependencies (`Nat.modEq_digits_sum`, `Nat.dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum`)
sections.mathContext: The proof depends on Mathlib's digit decomposition API: `Nat.digits b n` returns the base-$b$ digits of $n$, and `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` proves $n \equiv \text{digitsum}(n) \pmod{d}$ when $b \% d = 1$.

sections.title: Part I: Key Helper Lemmas
sections.summary: `base_mod_pred`: $b \% (b-1) = 1$ for $b \ge 3$, proved by rewriting $b = (b-1) + 1$ via `Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod`. `factor_mod`: for $d \ge 2$ with $d | (b-1)$, shows $b \% d = 1$ by writing $b = dk + 1$
sections.mathContext: These two lemmas establish the modular arithmetic foundation: $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ and $b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ for $d | (b-1)$. Everything else follows from Mathlib's digit sum congruence theorems.

sections.title: Part II: The Universal (b-1) Divisibility Rule
sections.summary: Three theorems: `modEq_digits_sum_base_minus_one` (congruence), `dvd_base_minus_one_iff` (divisibility iff), and `mod_base_minus_one_eq` (remainder equality). All are one-line applications of Mathlib APIs
sections.mathContext: $n \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{b-1}$ and $(b-1) | n \iff (b-1) | \sum d_i$. This is the universal digit sum rule.

sections.title: Part III: Divisibility by Factors of (b-1)
sections.summary: `dvd_factor_iff`: for any $d \ge 2$ dividing $(b-1)$, $d | n \iff d | \text{digitsum}_b(n)$. This generalizes the base-10 rules for 3 and 9 to arbitrary bases and factors
sections.mathContext: Since $d | (b-1) \implies b \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, the same digit sum congruence holds mod $d$: $n \equiv \sum d_i \pmod{d}$.

sections.title: Part IV: Specific Base Examples
sections.summary: Six concrete specializations: hex divisibility by 15, 3, 5; octal divisibility by 7; hex and octal remainder formulas. Each is a one-line instantiation of the general theorems
sections.mathContext: Hex: $16 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$, so $15 | n \iff 15 | \text{hexsum}(n)$; also $3 | 15$ and $5 | 15$ give digit sum tests for 3 and 5. Octal: $8 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$.

sections.title: Part VI: Cross-Base Divisibility
sections.summary: `cross_base_divisibility`: if $d | (b_1 - 1)$ and $d | (b_2 - 1)$, then digit sum divisibility is equivalent across bases. Example: $3 | \text{decsum}(n) \iff 3 | \text{hexsum}(n)$
sections.mathContext: The proof chains $d | \text{digitsum}_{b_1}(n) \iff d | n \iff d | \text{digitsum}_{b_2}(n)$, eliminating $n$ entirely.

sections.title: Part VII: Consistency with Parent
sections.summary: `consistent_div3` and `consistent_div9` reproduce the parent file's base-10 rules as special cases, confirming the generalization is backward-compatible
sections.mathContext: Base 10: $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$ and $3 | 9$, recovering the classical rules $9 | n \iff 9 | \text{digitsum}(n)$ and $3 | n \iff 3 | \text{digitsum}(n)$.

conclusion.summary: Complete formalization of base-$b$ divisibility rules with 0 axioms and 0 sorries across 15 theorems. The universal principle $b \equiv 1 \pmod{b-1}$ explains all digit-sum divisibility tests across all bases, unifying casting out nines (base 10), casting out sevens (base 8), and casting out fifteens (base 16) into a single theorem.
conclusion.implications: This formalization demonstrates that digit-sum divisibility rules are not base-specific tricks but instances of a universal principle in modular arithmetic. The cross-base theorem has practical implications: programmers can check divisibility by 3 using hex digit sums (useful when data is already in hexadecimal) with the same validity as decimal digit sums. The factor divisibility theorem generalizes further: any divisor of $(b-1)$ admits a digit sum test, explaining why base 10 has tests for 3 and 9 (both divide 9) but not for 7 (which doesn't divide 9).
openQuestions: Can the alternating digit sum rule (for $b+1$ and its factors) be formalized? Since $b \equiv -1 \pmod{b+1}$, we get $n \equiv \sum (-1)^i d_i \pmod{b+1}$, giving the rule for 11 in base 10
Can digit sum tests be extended to non-integer bases or mixed-radix representations?
Is there a formalization of the 'digital root' iteration (repeatedly summing digits until a single digit remains) as a fixed-point characterization of the residue mod $(b-1)$?
